rmt-2013-alg-01.title: Time budget
rmt-2013-alg-01.body:
Let a lap have length $d$. Four laps at $10$ mph take $\frac{4d}{10}=\frac{2d}5$ hours. The first three laps took $\frac{3d}9=\frac d3$ hours, leaving $\frac{2d}5-\frac d3=\frac d{15}$ hours for the last lap, so the speed must be $d\big/\frac d{15}=15$ mph.

**Answer: 15 mph**

rmt-2013-alg-02.title: Steady state
rmt-2013-alg-02.body:
The next dawn's amount must be at least $10$: $\frac{11}{10}(10-x)\ge10$, i.e. $10-x\ge\frac{100}{11}$, so $x\le\frac{10}{11}$. At equality the amount is the same each day, so the maximum is $x=\frac{10}{11}$.

**Answer: $\frac{10}{11}$ pounds**

rmt-2013-alg-03.title: Sum of coefficients is $p(1)$
rmt-2013-alg-03.body:
Such polynomials are $(x-r)(x-17)$ with $r$ an integer and $|r-17|\le17$, i.e. $0\le r\le34$ (the case $r=17$ is the double root). The sum of the coefficients is $p(1)=(1-r)(1-17)=16r-16$.

$\sum_{r=0}^{34}(16r-16)=16\cdot\frac{34\cdot35}{2}-16\cdot35=9520-560=8960$.

**Answer: 8960**

rmt-2013-alg-05.title: Discriminant
rmt-2013-alg-05.body:
Intersections satisfy $x^2+(2-b)x+20=0$, which has exactly one root when $(2-b)^2=80$, so $b=2\pm4\sqrt5$. Then $b_1^2+b_2^2=2(4+80)=168$.

**Answer: 168**

rmt-2013-alg-06.title: Factor
rmt-2013-alg-06.body:
$x^4-x^3-5x^2+2x+6=(x^2-2)(x^2-3)-x(x^2-2)=(x^2-2)(x^2-x-3)$. The roots are $\pm\sqrt2$ and $\frac{1\pm\sqrt{13}}2$. Since $\frac{1+\sqrt{13}}2>2>\sqrt2$, the largest root is $\frac{1+\sqrt{13}}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{1+\sqrt{13}}2$**

rmt-2013-alg-07.title: Monotonic iteration
rmt-2013-alg-07.body:
Let $f(a)=\sqrt[3]{20x+a}$, increasing in $a$. The equation is $f(f(13))=13$. If $f(13)>13$ then $f(f(13))>f(13)>13$, and if $f(13)<13$ then $f(f(13))<13$; so we need $f(13)=13$, i.e. $20x+13=13^3=2197$, giving $x=\frac{2184}{20}=\frac{546}5$.

**Answer: $\frac{546}5$**

rmt-2013-alg-08.title: Add a common term
rmt-2013-alg-08.body:
Let $f=4x^2+15x+17$, $g=x^2+4x+12$, $h=x^2+x+1$. The right side is $\frac{f+h}{g+h}$. Cross-multiplying, $\frac fg=\frac{f+h}{g+h}\Rightarrow fg+fh=fg+gh\Rightarrow h(f-g)=0$. Since $h>0$ for real $x$, $f=g$: $3x^2+11x+5=0$, discriminant $121-60=61>0$, so two real roots with sum $-\frac{11}3$.

**Answer: $-\frac{11}3$**

rmt-2013-alg-09.title: Symmetric simplification
rmt-2013-alg-09.body:
Over a common denominator $(a-b)(b-c)(a-c)$ the numerator $a^4(b-c)-b^4(a-c)+c^4(a-b)$ vanishes when $a=b$, $b=c$ or $a=c$, so it is divisible by $(a-b)(b-c)(a-c)$; the quotient is a symmetric quadratic, namely $a^2+b^2+c^2+ab+bc+ca$. (This is the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial $h_2(a,b,c)$, as in Lagrange interpolation.)

Now $a^2+b^2+c^2+ab+bc+ca=\frac12\big[(a+b)^2+(b+c)^2+(c+a)^2\big]$ with $a+b=2\sqrt7$, $b+c=2\sqrt3$, $c+a=2\sqrt5$, giving $\frac12(28+12+20)=30$.

**Answer: 30**

rmt-2013-alg-10.title: Gauss-period style
rmt-2013-alg-10.body:
If $z=1$ the sum is $6$. Otherwise let $\omega=z+z^3+z^4+z^9+z^{10}+z^{12}$ and use $1+z+\dots+z^{12}=0$. Squaring and reducing exponents mod $13$ gives $\omega^2=(z^2+z^5+z^6+z^7+z^8+z^{11})+2\cdot(\text{each of }z^1,\dots,z^{12}\text{ appearing twice in the cross terms, plus three constants})$, which simplifies to $\omega^2=3-\omega$. So $\omega=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{13}}2$, and both values occur (numerically, $z=e^{2\pi i k/13}$ gives $\approx1.303$ for $k=1,3,4,9,10,12$ and $\approx-2.303$ for the other nonzero $k$).

**Answer: $6,\ \frac{-1\pm\sqrt{13}}2$**
